extracted.intended_audience: educators, philanthropists, reformers, and general readers interested in Black education and Southern social policy (early 20th century)
extracted.subtask_description: A book chapter offering evaluative standards and prescriptive policy proposals concerning the education of Black Americans, the assessment of teachers and schools, and broader solutions to the 'Negro problem' in the U.S. South.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher evaluation — judge by results
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate test of efficiency of efforts is the result of effort. The teacher should be judged by whether he 'makes good' in results — does he do the thing he sets out to do, and does he do it well?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on extraneous criteria (recitation conduct, slips in diction/syntax, personal appearance, alma mater, number of degrees, moral character, church membership). These may have a place, but they do not strike the most salient point: measurable results produced by the teacher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional success measured by graduates' outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: A school's worth should be tested by the results accomplished by its graduates and ex-students; the school is willing to 'stand or fall by the results of our graduates.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep records of graduates and ex-students open for inspection; alumni accomplishments (employment, founding schools, civic improvement) serve as the primary metric of a school's effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum emphasis on practical/industrial arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial schools should train children in practical arts necessary to make an earnest, comfortable living — farming, blacksmithing, wheelwrighting, sewing, laundering, printing, domestic science, home nursing — rather than foreign languages or advanced mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus instruction on English and simple arithmetic; avoid spending time on subjects deemed impractical for the pupil population (higher mathematics, psychology, economics, sociology, logic) when the objective is preparing for local trades and livelihoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character formation and service orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Schools should inculcate thrift, industry, love for work, moral training, and a spirit of service; educators' personal example (e.g., Mr. Edwards's Christian life) is crucial in inspiring students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize moral and religious instruction alongside industrial training; encourage students to return and serve their communities (e.g., rural districts) after completing education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scholarships, prizes, and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarships and monetary prizes (e.g., Sumner Peace Prize; first and second prizes funded by alumni) are valuable tools to encourage achievement and sustain educational traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alumni or patrons can underwrite recurring prizes to motivate students; offering scholarships broadens access for deserving pupils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the 'Negro problem' as multi-dimensional
rubrics_metrics.description: The Negro problem comprises the economic, political, civil, and social status of twelve million people of African descent in the U.S.; any solution must address these dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proposed remedies by whether they produce improvements across economic, political, civil, and social spheres rather than focusing narrowly on one aspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of coercive and exclusionary White solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods such as teaching the Negro 'his place' via disfranchisement, limiting education, street/railroad discrimination, barring from public amenities, and ultimately lynchings are condemned as means of solving the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that such measures are both morally wrong and counterproductive — they foster resentment, injustice, and ultimately more crime and social instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of the 'master and Bible' remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that returning to the master-and-Bible model of slavery days will solve race problems is false; historical record shows the lash was more often used than the Bible and slavery produced profound race conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical evidence undermines nostalgic appeals to slavery-era paternalism; remedies must avoid romanticizing coercive past practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only true solution — compulsory education (ages 6–14) with religious, moral, and industrial training
rubrics_metrics.description: There is but one true solution: enact compulsory educational laws keeping all children between six and fourteen in school, providing religious, moral, and industrial training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also advocate a more equitable division of the school fund between races. Compulsory schooling combined with industrial instruction is presented as the central, practical policy to uplift the race and reduce crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable funding and support for Negro schools
rubrics_metrics.description: The Negro schools are 'the hope of the race' and require equitable division of school funds and continued philanthropic support, particularly from northern benefactors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philanthropists and friends should maintain sympathy, encouragement, and assistance; the record of these schools and their graduates should be made open to impartial inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation between best white people and best Negroes
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory solution requires agreement and joint effort by the best white people and the best class of Negroes about the aims and means of uplift (i.e., whether the Negro should 'know his place' or know the truth and be free).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mutual agreement on objectives is a prerequisite for effective policy; solutions imposed unilaterally by one side will fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social class analysis — prioritize support for constructive Negro classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Among three Negro classes described, the second class (renters, farmers, preachers, teachers, students, professionals, business men) is the constructive group that seeks education, property ownership, civic duty, and constitutional rights and therefore should be the focus of uplift efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies and resources should strengthen and expand this class, which works to quell riots, raise moral tone, and improve community conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemnation of violence and disenfranchisement as counterproductive
rubrics_metrics.description: Lynchings, mobs, deprivation of education, and disfranchisement do not solve problems but produce ignorance and increase crime; sowing hatred begets violent backlash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and civic remedies must avoid extralegal violence and discrimination; uphold justice in courts and equitable civic treatment to reduce lawlessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of soil fertility and agricultural conservation in the South
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest menace to the South is the loss of soil fertility; conservation and preservation of the soil is the region's most pressing need and will determine long-term prosperity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that temporary crop increases are due to bringing new acreage under cultivation rather than improved methods; unless soil conservation is adopted, farm production will decline as old lands become exhausted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative prioritization of social problems (child labor vs. soil loss)
rubrics_metrics.description: While problems like child labor negatively affect citizenship and future development, they are not identified as the single greatest menace compared to soil depletion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy makers should weigh and prioritize interventions; conserve soil as foundational to addressing other regional ills.
